title: My Calendar III
description:
# My Calendar III

A `k`-booking happens when `k` events share at least one common time point. The calendar stores half-open intervals `[start, end)`, so an event ending at time `t` does not overlap another event starting at time `t`.

Implement the `MyCalendarThree` class:

*   `MyCalendarThree()` Initializes an empty calendar.
*   `int book(int start, int end)` Adds the event `[start, end)` and returns the largest `k` such that some time point is covered by `k` booked events.

Store every booking, including overlaps and identical intervals. Return the greatest number of stored events covering a time point simultaneously.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1:

**Input**
["MyCalendarThree", "book", "book", "book", "book", "book", "book"]
[[], [10, 20], [50, 60], [10, 40], [5, 15], [5, 10], [25, 55]]
**Output**
[null, 1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3]
**Explanation**
MyCalendarThree myCalendarThree = new MyCalendarThree();
myCalendarThree.book(10, 20); // return 1
myCalendarThree.book(50, 60); // return 1
myCalendarThree.book(10, 40); // return 2, because [10,20) is covered by two events.
myCalendarThree.book(5, 15);  // return 3, because [10,15) is covered by three events.
myCalendarThree.book(5, 10);  // return 3, because this event touches the peak but does not increase it.
myCalendarThree.book(25, 55); // return 3

## Constraints:

*   `0 <= start < end <= 10^9`
*   At most `400` calls will be made to `book`.

solutions.name: TreeMap Sweep-Line Delta
solutions.description:
## Approach
Treat every booking as two sweep-line events: `+1` at `start` and `-1` at `end`. A `TreeMap` keeps all event points sorted. After inserting the new interval, scan the values in order, maintain the number of active intervals, and return the largest active count ever seen.

## Key Insight
The intervals are half-open. Placing `-1` at `end` means an interval ending at time `t` is removed before another interval starting at `t` contributes to the next open span, so adjacent events do not overlap. This is the direct generalization of counting overlaps with a difference array.

## Complexity Analysis
There can be at most `2n` distinct endpoints after `n` bookings. Each call scans them all, so the total time is `O(n^2)` over all calls and the space is `O(n)`.

solutions.name: Dynamic Segment Tree Range Add
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n log C) total, where C = 10^9
solutions.description:
## Approach
Build a segment tree lazily over the whole coordinate range `[0, 10^9]`. Each node stores `add`, the value added to the entire node interval, and `max`, the maximum overlap inside that interval after all updates. Booking `[start, end)` becomes a range add on `[start, end - 1]`, and the root maximum is the answer.

## Key Insight
The coordinate range is huge, but only paths touched by bookings need nodes. A node's best value is its own lazy add plus the better child maximum. That invariant lets the root answer the global maximum immediately after every update.

## Complexity Analysis
Each update visits `O(log C)` levels, so `n` bookings cost `O(n log C)` time. The tree allocates only visited nodes, giving `O(n log C)` worst-case space.

solutions.name: Coordinate Compression Difference Rebuild
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n^2 log n) total for n bookings
solutions.description:
## Approach
Keep all accepted intervals. After each new booking, collect every endpoint seen so far, sort them with a `TreeSet`, assign each endpoint a compressed index, and run a difference-array sweep on those compressed positions.

## Key Insight
The answer only changes at interval endpoints. The call limit is only 400, so rebuilding the compressed coordinate system on every call is simple, deterministic, and still comfortably fast for teaching the sweep-line idea without implementing a tree.

## Complexity Analysis
For the `i`-th booking, rebuilding and sweeping costs `O(i log i)`. Across all calls the total time is `O(n^2 log n)`, and the extra space is `O(n)`.

solutions.name: Ordered Disjoint Segment Counts
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n^2 log n) total for n bookings
solutions.description:
## Approach
Maintain a `TreeMap` whose keys split the timeline into disjoint segments. The value at a key is the booking count on the segment that starts there. Before adding a new interval, split at `start` and `end`, then increment every segment start in `[start, end)` and update the global best count.

## Key Insight
Once the map has boundaries at every relevant endpoint, each segment has a constant overlap count. This route exposes a different mental model from sweep-line deltas: instead of recomputing prefix sums, it mutates the actual covered spans.

## Complexity Analysis
Each booking may touch `O(n)` segments, and map navigation costs `O(log n)`, so the total worst-case time is `O(n^2 log n)`. The map stores at most two new boundaries per booking, so the space is `O(n)`.

solutions.name: Start-Endpoint Scan Baseline
solutions.description:
## Approach
Store every booking. After adding a new interval, examine each booked start time as a candidate point and count how many intervals cover it. The maximum count over those candidates is the answer.

## Key Insight
For half-open intervals, the maximum overlap is always achieved immediately after some start endpoint. Endpoints that only close intervals cannot create a new larger maximum. This makes the baseline much simpler than checking every integer time, while still being a useful correctness oracle for the optimized methods.

## Complexity Analysis
The `i`-th booking checks `i` candidate start times against `i` intervals, so the total time is `O(n^2)`. The stored intervals use `O(n)` space.
